Composite materials are increasingly used in the aerospace industry due to their superior mechanical properties and weight saving potentials.
Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymers (CFRP) are a composite made with carbon fibres embedded in a polymer.
CFRP is widely used in primary and secondary structures of civil and military aircraft.
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) declared a cap on CO emissions in 2009.
The ICAO aims to provide carbon-neutral growth and a 50% reduction in aviation CO2 emissions by 2050.
Unsuitable polymerisation conditions may lead to crack initiation in stringers.
Automated fibre placement can result in potential flaws such as gaps, laps, and twists.
Multi-material structures, such as aluminium bonded to CFRP, have excellent fatigue life, impact resistance, and residual strength characteristics.
Health diagnostics of composite patches are becoming important due to debonding under cyclic loading conditions.
Internal defects may be generated in composites during manufacture or in-service life.
Barely Visible Impact Damages (BVIDs) can cause a complex net of matrix cracking and delamination.
BVIDs often cause a significant reduction in the mechanical properties and fatigue resistance of composite structures.
The attenuation of waves propagating perpendicular to CRFP plies can provide information to identify and interpret interlaminar quality.
Phased array ultrasonic testing can increase the coverage area of sensors and compensate for misalignment between the probe and composite structure.
Laser generated ultrasound has the potential to monitor structures with complex curvatures.
Ultrasonic testing (UT) has limited resolution and is slow compared to other modalities.
